issues.legal_issue: A conviction may be sustained despite challenges to the timing of the first information report, the credibility of eyewitnesses, and alleged inconsistencies in the evidence when the record supports the prosecution account.
material_facts: The police general diary recorded the complaint and registration of the case on the evening of the incident, and the constable who delivered the special report had returned to the police station early the following morning.
The omission of some particulars from the material sent to the doctor and the absence of all accused persons’ names from a radio message did not establish that the report was delayed or fabricated.

The witnesses’ presence was supported by their being named in the complaint; one witness’s minor injury and explanation for remaining away from the village were accepted, and another witness was present in the village and had made the complaint.
The challenged witnesses were closely cross-examined over lengthy periods, and the courts found that the resulting contradictions, omissions, and improvements did not undermine their accounts.
The medical evidence supported the conclusion that the deceased died from injuries consistent with the weapons and manner of attack described by the eyewitnesses.
issues.conclusion: The appeals against conviction were dismissed, and the convictions and sentences upheld by the High Court were left undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: An asserted delay or fabrication of a first information report must be assessed against the full record; omissions of particulars from material sent for post-mortem do not by themselves establish that the report was antedated. Mahendra Rai v. Mithilesh Rai (1997) 10 SCC 605 supports the principle that the doctor need not receive every particular contained in the report or inquest papers. A witness’s connection with the deceased does not by itself make the witness unreliable, and contradictions or omissions arising in lengthy cross-examination must be assessed in context. Medical evidence consistent with the eyewitness account supports the prosecution case.

rule.if: conviction_appeal and report_timing_supported_by_records and eyewitness_presence_supported_by_record and witness_discrepancies_not_fatal and medical_evidence_consistent_with_account

predicates.conviction_appeal: The accused appealed a conviction entered after trial.
predicates.report_timing_supported_by_records: The contemporaneous records and surrounding circumstances supported the prosecution account of when the complaint was made and the report was sent.
predicates.eyewitness_presence_supported_by_record: The record, including an early complaint or other supporting circumstances, supported the claimed presence of the eyewitnesses.
predicates.witness_discrepancies_not_fatal: The inconsistencies in the eyewitness accounts did not materially undermine their credibility when assessed in the context in which they arose.
predicates.medical_evidence_consistent_with_account: The medical evidence was consistent with the injuries and manner of attack described by the prosecution witnesses.

issues.definition: When a convicted person appeals and the report timing, eyewitness presence, witness credibility, and medical evidence are supported in these ways, the conviction is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: A member of an unlawful assembly who shares its common object may be liable for the assembly’s killings even without proof that the member personally committed an assault.
material_facts: The State appealed the acquittal of two accused who had been convicted at trial.

The High Court accepted that the two accused were present with the other accused during the incident but acquitted them because the evidence did not show that they personally took part in the assault.
The trial court had found that the accused were members of an unlawful assembly with the common object of killing one of the deceased, and the High Court did not reject that finding.
The evidence accepted by the courts showed that the two accused had a motive, were present throughout with the group, and left with the others.
issues.conclusion: The State’s appeals were allowed, the acquittals were set aside, and the trial court’s convictions were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 149 IPC, a member of an unlawful assembly who shares its common object is liable for the offence committed in pursuit of that object even if no overt act is attributed to that member. The Court relied on Yunis alias Kariya v. State of M.P. (2003) 1 SCC 425, which holds that membership in the unlawful assembly is sufficient for liability when the charge is under Section 149 IPC.

rule.if: state_appeal_against_acquittal and accused_present_as_group and shared_common_object and unlawful_assembly_committed_killing and no_individual_assault_proved

predicates.state_appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed an acquittal entered by an appellate court.
predicates.accused_present_as_group: The accused were present with the group during the relevant incident.
predicates.shared_common_object: The accused were found to share the unlawful assembly’s common object.
predicates.unlawful_assembly_committed_killing: The unlawful assembly committed a killing in pursuit of its common object.
predicates.no_individual_assault_proved: The evidence did not establish that the accused personally carried out an assault.

issues.definition: When the prosecution appeals an acquittal and the accused were present as part of an assembly that shared and pursued a common object resulting in a killing, the acquittal is set aside and the trial conviction restored even if no personal assault was proved.
